warmup.q: A Kubernetes pod restarted. Its last state says Terminated, exit code 137. What does 137 tell you?
options: The process was killed by signal 9, SIGKILL, because 137 = 128 + 9
warmup.why: When a signal kills a process, shells and container runtimes report 128 plus the signal number. 137 is SIGKILL, which no program can catch: the grace period ran out, or the kernel's OOM killer stepped in. An uncaught OutOfMemoryError in main ends the JVM with status 1, and nobody writes System.exit(137) on purpose.

sections.h: A process is a running program with a record in the kernel
sections.html:
Lesson 1 of this track put the kernel in charge of every program on the machine. To be in charge, it has to keep notes. For each running program it must know which memory is that program's, which files it has open, who started it, whether it is running or waiting, and in the end how it finished. Without those notes the kernel couldn't stop one program from reading another's files, and it couldn't tell a shell whether ls worked.

A running program plus the kernel's notes about it is a process. Linux keeps the notes in a structure called task_struct. Each process gets a number, its PID (process ID), and records the PID of the process that created it, its parent, as its PPID. Every process except the very first was created by another one, so processes form a tree with PID 1 at the root.

You don't need a debugger to read the notes. Linux shows them as files under /proc/<pid>/. Here is head reading its own status file in the lab box:

Name:	head
State:	R (running)
Tgid:	12
Pid:	12
PPid:	1

PPid: 1 means the box's shell, PID 1, started head. (Tgid, the thread group ID, gets explained in lesson 3 of this track.)

The state says what the process is doing at this moment. ps shows it as one letter in its STAT column:

  • R: running, or ready to run as soon as a CPU is free
  • S: asleep until something happens, such as a timer, data on a socket or a child exiting
  • D: asleep in a way that can't be interrupted, usually waiting for a disk
  • T: stopped
  • Z: a zombie, dead and waiting for its parent (section 3 explains)

Every process takes the same path through its life, and this lesson walks it in order. A parent creates it (fork). It loads the program it should run (exec). It ends (exit). Its parent collects how it ended (wait). While it lives, other processes can send it signals. Keep that picture of a tree of rows in the kernel's table, each row moving through create, run, end and collect. The stepper in the next section shows one row make the whole trip, and the lab has you build the table.

try.title: Read a process's record
steps: From the labs folder, start the lab box: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box.
Run the commands below. $! holds the PID of the last command you started in the background with &.
Before the grep, predict the state of a process that is running sleep 100.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: head -9 /proc/self/status ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd sleep 100 & grep -E '^(State|PPid)' /proc/$!/status kill $!

try.expect:
PIDs will differ:

Name:	head
Umask:	0022
State:	R (running)
Tgid:	12
Ngid:	0
Pid:	12
PPid:	1
TracerPid:	0
Uid:	0	0	0	0
  PID  PPID STAT CMD
    1     0 Ss   bash -l
   13     1 R    ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd
State:	S (sleeping)
PPid:	1

head and ps are R because they were running when they looked at themselves. sleep is S: it's waiting for a timer and uses no CPU. In the Ss of the shell, the small s marks a session leader. The Mac has no /proc, though ps -o pid,ppid,stat,command works there too.

sections.h: fork copies a process, exec replaces its program
sections.html:
A shell has to run ls -l > files.txt: start ls, and send its output to a file instead of the terminal. The simplest design is one system call, say spawn("/usr/bin/ls", args), that creates a process already running ls. It works for plain ls. It breaks for > files.txt, because ls should write to a file, so spawn needs a parameter for where output goes. Then one for input, one for a pipe between two programs, one for the working directory, the environment variables, the user, the resource limits. Every new kind of setup becomes another parameter.

Unix took a different route in the 1970s, and Linux kept it. Creating a process is split into two calls, with your own code running in between.

fork() makes a copy of the calling process. The child gets a new PID. Everything else starts as a copy of the parent: the code, the memory, the open files and the signal handlers (section 4 explains signals). Both processes return from the same fork() call. The parent gets the child's PID and the child gets 0, and that is how each one knows which it is. Copying all the memory sounds slow for a big process, but the kernel shares the memory and copies a page only when one side writes to it. Lesson 7 of this track covers that copy-on-write trick.

execve() replaces the program running in a process. The kernel throws away the old code and memory and loads a new program from disk. The PID stays, and so do the parent and the open files. A successful execve never returns, because the code that called it is gone.

The gap between the two is the point. After fork, the child still runs the shell's code, so it can change things about itself before it becomes ls. Open files are named by file descriptors, small numbers where 1 is standard output (lesson 1 of this track). To redirect, the child opens the file and makes descriptor 1 refer to it with dup2. Here is the heart of tinysh.c, a 50-line shell in the labs folder:

pid_t pid = fork();                     // 1. copy this process
if (pid == 0) {                         // child: still tinysh's code
    int fd = open(file, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644);
    dup2(fd, 1);                        // make fd 1 the file
    close(fd);
    execvp(argv[0], argv);              // 2. replace the program
    _exit(127);                         // only reached if exec failed
}
waitpid(pid, &status, 0);               // 3. wait, collect the status

ls knows nothing about files: it writes to descriptor 1, as always. The shell pointed descriptor 1 at the file before ls started. Pipes, environment variables and limits use the same gap, and spawn never needs a parameter for them.

The third call closes the loop. wait() (on Linux the system call is wait4) lets the parent sleep until a child ends and then hands it the child's exit status, the number the child passed to exit() (0 means success). That's where $? in bash and Process.waitFor() in Java get their number.

You won't find a fork system call in an arm64 trace. glibc's fork() calls clone with the flag SIGCHLD and without CLONE_THREAD, which means "a new process, and tell the parent when it dies". Java's ProcessBuilder.start() takes yet another road on Linux, through posix_spawn and a small helper program, jspawnhelper, and ends in the same execve and the same wait4.

steps: In the box, build the shell: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/tinysh os/c/l02/tinysh.c. Read os/c/l02/tinysh.c on your Mac while it compiles. It is 50 lines.

Now trace it. Run the first command below, type ls os > /tmp/listing.txt and then exit, and print the trace with the second command.

sections.h: A dead child stays a zombie until its parent waits
sections.html:
A parent often needs to know how its child ended. bash needs it for $?, a build tool needs it to stop on the first failed step, and ProcessBuilder needs it for waitFor(). But the child may finish long before the parent asks. Where does the answer wait in the meantime?

The simplest design deletes everything when a process exits. Then the exit status is gone before the parent asks. The next simplest keeps the whole process around until the parent asks. That wastes its memory and open files, possibly for hours. Linux does something in between. At exit it frees the memory and closes the files at once, and keeps only the small record with the PID and the exit status. A process in that state is a zombie. ps shows it as Z and <defunct>. It uses no CPU and almost no memory, and you can't kill it, because it is already dead. When the parent calls wait, the kernel hands over the status and deletes the record. That last step is called reaping.

The kernel tells the parent about the death with SIGCHLD, a signal (section 4). A shell or a JVM reacts by calling wait. A parent that never waits collects zombies, and each zombie keeps holding a PID.

Now flip the order. If the parent dies first, the child is an orphan. It keeps running, but nobody is left to wait for it. So the kernel gives it a new parent: PID 1, or the nearest ancestor that registered as a "subreaper" (a process that asked the kernel, through prctl, to adopt the orphans below it). When the orphan exits, PID 1 has to reap it. On most Linux servers PID 1 is systemd, which reaps every orphan it gets.

In a container, PID 1 is whatever program the image starts. If that is your JVM, nobody reaps orphans. The JVM waits for the children it started with ProcessBuilder and ignores every other process that ends up under it. I ran a JVM as PID 1 that started sh -c 'sleep 1 & exit 0'. The shell exited, its sleep became the JVM's orphan, and a few seconds later:

  PID  PPID STAT CMD
    1     0 Ssl  java /exp/Orphaner.java
   30     1 Z    [sleep] <defunct>

One zombie is harmless. A service that shells out to a PDF converter through a wrapper script that backgrounds things leaks one PID per call. The container's limit on PIDs counts threads too (lesson 3 of this track), so eventually the JVM can't even start a thread. docker run --init, or tini as the entrypoint, puts a tiny init program in front of yours. It reaps orphans and passes signals on.

try.title: Make a zombie and an orphan
steps: In the box, build the two programs in os/c/l02/: zombie.c exits its child at once and waits 10 seconds before reaping it, and orphan.c exits the parent while its child still runs.
Run the commands below. The second ps comes 10 seconds after the first.
Predict the PPID the orphan reports after its parent exits.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/zombie os/c/l02/zombie.c gcc -O2 -o /tmp/orphan os/c/l02/orphan.c /tmp/zombie 10 & sleep 1; ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd sleep 10; ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd /tmp/orphan

try.expect:
parent 57 forked child 59; reaping it in 10 s
  PID  PPID STAT CMD
    1     0 Ss   bash -l
   57     1 S    /tmp/zombie 10
   59    57 Z    [zombie] <defunct>
   60     1 R    ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd
parent reaped 59, exit status 7
  PID  PPID STAT CMD
    1     0 Ss   bash -l
   62     1 R    ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd
child 64: my parent is 63
parent 63: exiting without waiting
child 64: my parent is now 1

For 10 seconds PID 59 is a Z with its parent's PID next to it. Once the parent calls waitpid it gets status 7 and the zombie is gone. The orphan's parent changes from 63 to 1, the box's bash. bash calls wait for any child it has, so the orphan is reaped when it exits.

sections.h: SIGTERM asks a process to stop, SIGKILL doesn't ask
sections.html:
Sooner or later something has to tell your service to stop: a deploy, a scale-down, a person at a terminal. How?

The bluntest way is for the kernel to remove the process on request. It always works, and it is a disaster for a payment service in the middle of a settlement batch: half-written files, uncommitted Kafka offsets, requests cut off mid-flight. A better way is to send the process a message and let its own code decide what to do: finish the work in hand, flush, then exit. That message is a signal, a small numbered notice the kernel delivers to a process. Some signals come from the kernel itself, such as SIGSEGV for a bad memory access or SIGCHLD when a child dies. Others come from another process through the kill system call, which sends any signal, despite its name.

For each signal, a process has a disposition: do the default action, ignore it, or run a handler, a function the program registered for that signal. For most signals the default action is to end the process.

Handlers bring their own failure: a buggy or stuck program could catch the stop request and never stop. So Linux keeps two signals that no program can catch, block or ignore: SIGKILL (9) and SIGSTOP (19). The kernel acts on them without asking the program. That gives you both tools. SIGTERM (15) asks politely, and SIGKILL is the blunt removal for when asking fails.

The JVM registers handlers for SIGTERM, SIGINT (2, what Ctrl-C sends) and SIGHUP (1). When one arrives, it runs your shutdown hooks, so Quarkus can stop taking requests, a Kafka consumer can commit its offsets and a logger can flush. Then it exits with status 143. SIGKILL gets none of that:

$ kill -TERM $!; wait $!; echo "exit status: $?"
shutdown hook: flushed 3 pending ledger entries
exit status: 143
$ kill -KILL $!; wait $!; echo "exit status: $?"
exit status: 137

Where do 143 and 137 come from? An exit code is one byte. When a signal kills a process, wait reports "killed by signal N" instead of an exit code, and bash folds that into one number for $?: 128 + N. So 137 is 128 + 9 and 143 is 128 + 15. Java's Process.exitValue() follows the same rule. The JVM's 143 after SIGTERM is a real exit code: its handler caught the signal, ran the hooks, and then exited with the number a shell would have shown anyway.

docker stop uses both tools in order. It sends SIGTERM to the container's PID 1, waits 10 seconds by default, then sends SIGKILL. Kubernetes does the same with a default grace period of 30 seconds. So exit code 137 on a pod means something used SIGKILL: either the grace period ran out, or the kernel's out-of-memory (OOM) killer ended the process for using too much memory (lesson 7 of this track).

try.title: SIGTERM against SIGKILL on a JVM
steps: Read os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java. It installs a shutdown hook and sleeps for a minute, like a settlement batch.
In the box, start it in the background, send SIGTERM, and print the exit status. Then do the same with SIGKILL. The sleep 2 gives the JVM time to compile and start the file.
Predict both exit statuses and whether the hook's line prints each time.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: java os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java & sleep 2; kill -TERM $!; wait $!; echo "exit status: $?" java os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java & sleep 2; kill -KILL $!; wait $!; echo "exit status: $?"

try.expect:
pid 66: settlement batch running
shutdown hook: flushed 3 pending ledger entries
exit status: 143
pid 92: settlement batch running
exit status: 137
bash: line 25:    92 Killed                  java os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java

SIGTERM reached the JVM's handler, the hook ran, and the JVM exited with 143. SIGKILL never reached the program. The kernel ended it, the hook never ran, and bash reported "Killed" and 137. (Your bash's line number will differ.)

analogy: Think of each child process as a CompletableFuture its parent started. fork plus exec is the supplyAsync call, the exit status is the result, and wait is get(). A zombie is a future that has completed but whose result nobody has read: the work is done and the slot is still taken. An orphan is a future whose owner went away, so a caretaker (PID 1) takes it over and promises to read it. A signal is cancel(), and SIGKILL is a cancel() the task can't intercept. The analogy breaks on cleanup. An unread future is garbage collected once nothing refers to it. A zombie never goes away on its own. The kernel keeps it until somebody calls wait, however long that takes.
world: Your services go through this lesson on every deploy. Kubernetes stops a pod by sending SIGTERM to PID 1 in each container, waiting terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 by default), then sending SIGKILL. Quarkus uses the SIGTERM window for a graceful shutdown: stop taking HTTP requests, let in-flight card authorizations finish, commit Kafka offsets. Two things break it. If the image's entrypoint is a shell that doesn't exec the JVM, the SIGTERM lands on the shell and is dropped (the worked example shows it happen), so every deploy ends in SIGKILL and exit 137 and in-flight work is cut off. And if shutdown takes longer than the grace period, for example a Temporal worker waiting for a long activity to finish, you also get SIGKILL. When a pod shows 137 and its log has no shutdown lines, check the entrypoint first, then the grace period, then memory.
mistake: Using kill -9 as the normal way to stop a service. People reach for it because it always works. SIGKILL skips every shutdown hook: buffered log lines are lost, a Kafka consumer doesn't commit its last offsets so the next consumer processes those messages again, open Oracle transactions are cut off and rolled back, and the load balancer keeps sending requests until health checks notice. Send SIGTERM (plain kill <pid>), wait for the process to exit, and use kill -9 only on a process that ignored SIGTERM for longer than its grace period. Even then it has limits: it does nothing to a zombie, which is already dead, and a process stuck in D state may not die until its disk wait ends.

compare.title: The same JVM, stopped with SIGTERM and with SIGKILL

a.label: kill -TERM
a.title: lab box
a.html:
$ java os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java &
pid 66: settlement batch running
$ kill -TERM $!; wait $!; echo "exit status: $?"
shutdown hook: flushed 3 pending ledger entries
exit status: 143

b.label: kill -KILL
b.title: lab box
b.html:
$ java os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java &
pid 92: settlement batch running
$ kill -KILL $!; wait $!; echo "exit status: $?"
exit status: 137
bash: line 25:    92 Killed                  java os/src/demo/...

compare.note: SIGTERM is a request. The JVM has a handler for it, runs the shutdown hooks and then exits with 143 (128 + 15) by its own choice. SIGKILL is not delivered to the program at all: the kernel ends the process, and wait reports "killed by signal 9", which bash shows as 137. From the outside the two numbers look alike. Only the first one gave your code a chance to finish its work.

worked.title: Why didn't the shutdown hook run on docker stop?

steps.say: A ledger service's Dockerfile uses the shell form, ENTRYPOINT java -jar ledger.jar, which Docker runs as /bin/sh -c "...". Reproduce it with the demo and a shell that runs two commands. Then look at the process tree inside: sh is PID 1 and the JVM is its child.
steps.code: docker run -d --name sfz-os02-stop -v "$PWD":/labs sfz-labbox:1 \ sh -c "echo starting; java /labs/os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java" docker exec sfz-os02-stop ps -o pid,ppid,cmd # PID PPID CMD # 1 0 sh -c echo starting; java /labs/os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java # 7 1 java /labs/os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java

steps.say: Stop it with a 3 second grace period. The stop takes the full 3 seconds, the hook's line is missing from the log, and the exit code is 137.
steps.code: time docker stop -t 3 sfz-os02-stop # 3.11 s total docker logs sfz-os02-stop # starting # pid 7: settlement batch running docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}}' sfz-os02-stop # 137 docker rm sfz-os02-stop

steps.say: Why: Docker sent SIGTERM to PID 1, which is sh. The kernel protects a container's PID 1: it delivers a signal from outside only if PID 1 installed a handler for it, and sh has none for SIGTERM. So the signal was dropped. sh doesn't pass signals to its children anyway. After 3 seconds Docker sent SIGKILL, which the kernel always delivers. When a container's PID 1 dies, the kernel kills every other process in it, and the JVM died without running its hooks.

Fix: make the JVM itself PID 1. Use the exec form, ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "ledger.jar"], or end a wrapper script with exec java ... so the shell replaces itself with the JVM. The JVM has a SIGTERM handler, so the signal arrives. Same test with exec:
steps.code: docker run -d --name sfz-os02-stop -v "$PWD":/labs sfz-labbox:1 \ sh -c "echo starting; exec java /labs/os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l02/demo/GracefulShutdown.java" time docker stop -t 3 sfz-os02-stop # 0.11 s total docker logs sfz-os02-stop # starting # pid 1: settlement batch running # shutdown hook: flushed 3 pending ledger entries docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}}' sfz-os02-stop # 143 docker rm sfz-os02-stop

steps.say: If the JVM starts child processes, add --init too (in Kubernetes, put tini in the image as the entrypoint). The tiny init becomes PID 1, passes SIGTERM on to the JVM and reaps any orphans, so you get both a clean shutdown and no zombies.
steps.code: ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/tini", "--", "java", "-jar", "ledger.jar"]

lab.title: Model the kernel's process table
steps: Open ProcessTable.kt. fork, exec and handle are written for you. Read them first, and note what fork copies and what exec resets.
Run the tests from the labs folder. All ten fail.
Write shellCode: one when over the two kinds of ExitStatus.
Write exit through a private helper, terminate(p, status), that marks the process a zombie, re-parents its children to PID 1 and, if initReaps is true, removes every zombie whose parent is now PID 1.
Write kill. Handle the cases in the KDoc order: missing PID, zombie, SIGKILL, a handled signal, SIGCHLD, everything else. The death cases call terminate.
Write waitpid. Find the children of parent (only child if it isn't -1). None at all is ECHILD. If one is a zombie, remove it and return its PID and status. Otherwise return null.
Run the tests until all ten pass. The last test is the JVM-as-PID-1 story from this lesson.
hints: check(condition) { "ECHILD: ..." } throws an IllegalStateException with your message, which is what the tests look for.
Re-parent before you reap. A child that was already a zombie becomes init's zombie, and a reaping init removes it in the same step.
Collect the PIDs to remove into a list first, then remove them. Removing entries from table while you loop over table.values throws ConcurrentModificationException.
Test SIGKILL before the handler set. A program can't install a handler for it, but kill should not even look.

drill.title: fork, exec and wait in C, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write C that runs ls -l in a child process, waits for it, and prints either its exit code or the signal that killed it along with the number bash would show. Then say why the child calls _exit and not exit when exec fails.

answer.html: pid_t pid = fork(); if (pid < 0) { perror("fork"); exit(1); } if (pid == 0) { // child execlp("ls", "ls", "-l", (char *)NULL); perror("exec"); // only runs if exec failed _exit(127); // skip the stdio buffers and atexit } // handlers copied from the parent int status; waitpid(pid, &status, 0); // parent: sleep until the child ends if (WIFEXITED(status)) printf("exit code %d\n", WEXITSTATUS(status)); else if (WIFSIGNALED(status)) printf("signal %d, bash shows %d\n", WTERMSIG(status), 128 + WTERMSIG(status));

recap: A process is a running program plus the kernel's record of it: PID, parent, state, memory, open files and signal settings. /proc/<pid>/status shows the record.
fork copies the caller, execve replaces the program but keeps the PID and open files, and wait collects the exit status. The gap between fork and exec is where a shell sets up redirection.
A dead process stays a zombie (Z) until its parent waits. Orphans get PID 1 as their new parent, and PID 1 must reap them.
In a container your program may be PID 1. A JVM there doesn't reap orphans, and a shell there drops SIGTERM. Use the exec form, and --init when you start child processes.
SIGTERM can be caught, so the JVM runs its shutdown hooks and exits 143. SIGKILL can't, so nothing runs and the shell shows 137.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why our pods sometimes stop with exit code 137 on a normal deploy, while the same service stopped locally with Ctrl-C shuts down cleanly. Explain what is going on and what you would check.
explain.answer: 137 means the process was killed by signal 9, SIGKILL, because shells and container runtimes report 128 plus the signal number. SIGKILL can't be caught, so the JVM's shutdown hooks never ran. Locally, Ctrl-C sends SIGINT, which the JVM catches and handles by running the hooks. On a deploy, Kubernetes first sends SIGTERM to PID 1 and only sends SIGKILL after the grace period. So either the SIGTERM never reached the JVM, or shutdown took too long. I'd check the entrypoint first: if PID 1 is a shell that doesn't exec java, the kernel drops SIGTERM because the shell has no handler for it, and the JVM only ever sees SIGKILL. Then I'd check whether shutdown fits in terminationGracePeriodSeconds. If both are fine, I'd look for an OOM kill, which also shows up as 137.

deeper.html:
ProcessBuilder.start() on Linux doesn't call fork. Copying a JVM with a large heap and dozens of threads, even with copy-on-write, is wasteful when the child is about to exec anyway. Since JDK 13 (JDK-8213192) the default on Linux is posix_spawn, and the JDK runs a small helper, jspawnhelper, which then execs your command. Here is a trace of new ProcessBuilder("ls", "/labs").start() on JDK 25 in the lab box (trimmed):

39    clone3({flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_VFORK|CLONE_CLEAR_SIGHAND, exit_signal=SIGCHLD, ...}, 88) = -1 ENOSYS (Function not implemented)
39    clone(child_stack=0xffffb85ed000, flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_VFORK|SIGCHLD <unfinished ...>
59    execve("/opt/java/openjdk/lib/jspawnhelper", ["/opt/java/openjdk/lib/jspawnhelp"..., "25.0.5+8-LTS", "10:11:13"], ...) = 0
59    execve("/usr/bin/ls", ["ls", "/labs"], ...) = 0
39    --- SIGCHLD {si_signo=SIGCHLD, si_code=CLD_EXITED, si_pid=59, si_uid=0, si_status=0, si_utime=0, si_stime=0} ---
60    wait4(59, [{WIFEXITED(s) && WEXITSTATUS(s) == 0}], 0, NULL) = 59

CLONE_VM|CLONE_VFORK is the vfork pattern: the child shares the parent's memory instead of copying it, and the parent thread is paused until the child calls execve. Nothing is copied, so it costs the same for a 100 MB JVM as for a 30 GB one. (The clone3 and ENOSYS pair is Docker's seccomp again, from lesson 1.) The wait4 comes from thread 60, the JDK's "process reaper" thread, which waits for each child the JVM started and completes the Process.onExit() future. That thread is the reason a JVM reaps its own children and nobody else's.

Two more details are worth knowing. /proc/<pid>/status has bitmasks of the signals a process blocks, ignores and catches (SigBlk, SigIgn, SigCgt). For the demo JVM, SigCgt decodes to SIGHUP, SIGQUIT, SIGILL, SIGBUS, SIGFPE, SIGSEGV, SIGUSR2, SIGPIPE, SIGTERM and SIGXFSZ, plus two real-time signals. The JVM catches SIGSEGV on purpose, as part of how it handles null checks and safepoints, and SIGQUIT (kill -3) makes it print a thread dump, which lesson 3 of this track uses. And SIGINT was missing from that mask: bash starts background jobs with SIGINT ignored, and the JVM leaves an ignored signal ignored. A kill -INT to that background JVM did nothing at all.
